title: The Scout’s Blind Spot: Which Small-Sample Stars Might Mislead Chennai Super Kings?
dek: A batter who scores at a blistering rate from a handful of balls is the easiest player to over-rate. The IPL's history shows how far those small-sample stars fall back.
excerpt: Batters who scored far faster than average from fewer than a hundred balls kept only part of that edge the next season. Batters who did it over a full season kept somewhat more. Hot seasons of any size regress, and small ones are the easiest to over-read.
author: CricField Editorial Desk

sections.heading: The Small-Sample Star
body: A few explosive innings can make a batter look like a star. Scouts know the numbers are noisy, but the pull of a strike rate far above average is strong.
CricField took every IPL batter season with thirty to ninety-nine balls and a strike rate at least twenty per cent above the season average, and looked at the next season.

Batters with an equally hot season over two hundred and fifty balls or more averaged {{ev:bs-bb}} and then {{ev:bs-ba}}, keeping {{ev:bs-keep-big}} of their edge.

sections.heading: At CSK
body: {{ev:bs-mine}} of the small-sample hot seasons were for Chennai Super Kings. Each is a case where the numbers looked better than the evidence behind them.

sections.heading: Why This Happens
body: Large-sample hot seasons kept somewhat more of their edge than small-sample ones. Volume of evidence matters, but even full seasons regress.

Over a few dozen balls, luck in which deliveries go for six and which go to fielders dominates; over hundreds of balls, skill matters more. Some of the fall-back is bowlers adjusting to a new player. The Bayesian-shrinkage article in this series shows how to correct for it.

sections.heading: CricField Verdict: Shrink Before You Spend
body: Chennai Super Kings should discount small-sample strike rates heavily towards the average before bidding.
A full season of evidence is worth far more than a hot month.

methodology: Built from the CricField warehouse (Cricsheet ball-by-ball data, regulation innings). Generated by scripts/editorial/engine. Relative strike rate = runs ÷ (balls × season-average runs per ball) × 100. Hot = 120 or more; next season requires at least 60 balls.
